1.pericope_label: Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment... And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken

schools.summary: Ellicott would render the opening the king, and calls him the true Anointed one of the future, though not without reference to Hezekiah as the partial embodiment of the idea, which the mention of princes worthy of their king only strengthens; he marks the first eight verses off as standing to the preceding chapter exactly as the earlier picture of an ideal king stands to the anti-Assyrian prophecy before it. On the second verse he observes that the word for man is used elsewhere for a mighty or great man and probably keeps that sense, so the nobles of Judah, who had been tyrannous and oppressive, should become a true aristocracy, beneficent and protecting; he sees in the images the two great blessings of an Eastern landscape, streams that turn desert into oasis and a rock throwing its shadow against the noonday heat, and notices that the word for rock is the one applied to Assyria a few verses earlier, chosen to point the contrast. On the opened eyes he speaks of another reversal of the judicial blindness with which the prophet's commission had begun. Delitzsch says no physical miracle is predicted but a spiritual change, the judgment of hardening repealed and the defects of those not among the worst healed.

Gill refuses the Jewish reading that makes the king Hezekiah, allowing that king at most the place of a type, and takes the words of Christ himself, whose sceptre is a sceptre of righteousness; on the second verse he takes the man for the King Messiah just named, a hiding place from the wind of his Father's wrath, which he bore in his people's room. Calvin says the prediction undoubtedly relates to Hezekiah, under whom the Church was reformed after a wicked predecessor had overturned government and religion together, but that the prophet means to lead us farther, since the restoration only shadowed out there was fulfilled in Christ; he keeps the king in view at the second verse and argues that since many rulers by tyranny raise more troubles than they allay, the good king deserves this peculiar commendation, and what was said truly of Hezekiah may be said much more of Christ; and he sets the opened eyes against the dreadful threatening of an earlier chapter that God would blind them.

Clarke leans to Hezekiah as the primary subject, yet grants that in their fullest sense the words cannot be applied to any man, since God alone can do all that is promised; he praises the shadow of a great projecting rock as the most refreshing shade possible in a hot country, since it not only excludes the sun but has a natural coolness of its own; and he alone works on the text, proposing that a negative particle be read as a pronoun instead, a confusion the Masoretes acknowledge in fifteen places, since removing the negative restores the verb its usual sense. Wesley makes the king Hezekiah, a type of Christ and Christ typified by him, agrees that each of the princes is meant by the man, a shelter from the rage of evil men to the people under his government, and keeps the last verse practical, that they will no longer shut their eyes and ears against the good counsels of a religious king.
Henry takes the passage as a description of a flourishing kingdom, readable as a directory to magistrates and subjects, a panegyric on a good reign, and a direction to look for the kingdom of Christ.

debates.question: Who is the king that reigns in righteousness?

positions.view: Christ himself; Hezekiah is at most a type.
Hezekiah primarily, though in their fullest sense the words fit no man at all.
Hezekiah undoubtedly, but the prophet leads farther, the restoration being fulfilled in Christ.
The true Anointed one of the future, with Hezekiah as the partial present embodiment.
Hezekiah, a type of Christ and Christ typified by him.
Both at once: a good reign described, and the kingdom of Christ to be looked for.

debates.question: Who is the man who shall be a hiding place?

positions.view: The King Messiah just named, sheltering his people from his Father's wrath.
The nobles of Judah, turned from oppressors into a true and protecting aristocracy.
Each of the king's princes, a shelter to the people under his government.
The good king himself, whose worth is measured against rulers who raise more troubles than they allay.

outliers.note: Removes a negative from the text on the ground that the Masoretes themselves acknowledge fifteen instances of the same confusion, which reverses the sense of the clause.

themes: Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment.
And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.
And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken.

4.pericope_label: The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly... But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the heart the intellect rather than the emotions, the rash those hurried and reckless, the stammerers those with no power to speak clearly of divine things; he would render the second of the disputed words noble and the fourth gentle, matching them to the Greek and Latin words for a gentleman, and observes that this exactly reverses the picture at the opening of the prophet's work, where men called good evil and evil good. He says that in that better day men would learn to see one another as they are and not as they pretend, specifies the error the fool utters as heresy, hollow profession, or open scoffing, any of which comes out in practice as violence toward the poor, and adds that words so generic may still carry an implied reference to the men who had treated the prophet that way, making even him an offender for a word. Delitzsch states the principle governing the rest: a third fruit of the blessing is the naming and treating of every man according to his true character.

Gill takes the rash for men who never gave themselves time to consider what was proposed to them, hears the Hebrew play in the pair of names and applies it, that men ignorant of spiritual things shall not be made rulers in God's house, holds that a man without understanding of gospel truths can only speak foolish things about the sufficiency of his own righteousness, and rejects the readings that make the churl's instruments his measures, which two rabbis adopted, or his servants, preferring the evil methods by which covetous shepherds fleece the flock. Calvin explains why misnaming happens at all: when public government is wicked, covetous men are in power and honoured, because people judge virtue by wealth, so a poor man is despised though truly upright; good government detects the pretences quickly, since where virtue is esteemed vices are exposed. He insists on the future tense, that the prophet does not inquire what wicked men are but declares they shall be revealed under the reign of Christ, the heavenly light arising to expose hidden wickedness; and he allows measures for the instruments but thinks instrument the more extensive word.

Clarke gives each of the three names a portrait: the vile person is the pampered, brainless fellow who eats to live and lives to eat, giving little and that with an evil eye; the liberal is the openhearted, princely man who writes on all his possessions that they are for himself and mankind; the churl is the avaricious man who starves amid his plenty. He calls the following verse a proverbial saying which a Greek dramatist expressed in the very same words, that the fool speaks folly, takes the churl's instruments for machinations and designs, and judges that in the next clause a word has been lost and two others slightly altered, making the sentence very obscure. Wesley says the people's haste in judging was an argument of ignorance, and that the tongue which spoke of divine things darkly was only partly mended in the good king's day and truly changed by Christ; he makes the reversal plainest of all, that men shall no longer be miscalled, since everyone will discover what he is by his words and actions.

debates.question: Does the passage promise a change in men or a disclosure of them?

positions.view: A disclosure: the prophet declares that the wicked shall be revealed under Christ's reign, not that they will alter.
A disclosure: men would learn to see one another as they are and not as they pretend.
A disclosure: men shall no longer be miscalled, since each will show what he is by his words and actions.
The naming and treating of every man according to his true character, as a fruit of the blessing.
A change in office: men ignorant of spiritual things will no longer be made rulers in God's house.

debates.question: What are the instruments of the churl?

positions.view: Not his measures, nor his servants, but the methods by which covetous shepherds fleece the flock.
Measures would pass, but instrument is the more extensive word.
Machinations and designs; and the clause after them is textually corrupt.

outliers.note: Suggests that the generic words about destroying the poor with lying words may carry an implied reference to those who had treated the prophet himself so, making him an offender for a word.

themes: The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly.
The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful.

For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the Lord, to make empty the soul of the hungry, and he will cause the drink of the thirsty to fail.
The instruments also of the churl are evil: he deviseth wicked devices to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right.
But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand.

9.pericope_label: Rise up, ye women that are at ease; hear my voice, ye careless daughters... Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns and briers; yea, upon all the houses of joy in the joyous city

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the address to the women for a distinct sermon against evils the prophet had denounced long before, which continued unabated in spite of the reformation, and thinks it stands here because it paints the harem influence that lay behind the counsels of the king and his ministers. He reads the phrase about days and years as implying not the trouble's long continuance but its quick arrival, like our own saying about a year and a day; takes the failing vintage figuratively, since a truer insight into a poet-prophet's language would see the failure of every earthly joy where others see only a lost vine crop; finds a parallel and a contrast in the words spoken to the daughters of Jerusalem on the way to the cross; and adds that the forms of the summons are masculine, so the call is not limited to the women. Delitzsch prints the whole sequence, from this summons to the outpouring of the Spirit, as one continuous passage.

Gill reports that some take the men of the nation to be so called for their effeminacy and that the Jewish expositors understand the cities of Judea, the ancient paraphrase rendering it provinces; he gives the disputed phrase as days above a year and reports the readings that apply it either to the interval before the troubles or to their continuance; he allows the call to tremble as either exhortation or prediction; and he keeps the received word at the close, offering the teats of cattle dried by drought, the breasts of women that yield no milk in famine, or the fields themselves. Calvin agrees the words appear unconnected with what precedes but finds no absurdity in joining them, since the prophets commonly turn to hypocrites once grace is promised to believers; he is emphatic that the calamity will be long, since when no end is held out what is left but despair; and he defends the repetition, observing that men are in more danger from prosperity than adversity, flattering themselves when matters go smoothly.

Clarke adopts the ancient paraphrase outright and reads the address as made to provinces and cities, adding that from here to the fourteenth verse the desolation by the Chaldeans appears to be foretold; he observes that the word for sackcloth is necessary to the sense but has dropped out of our text, being preserved in the Greek and other versions, that the verbs are infinitives to be taken imperatively, and that the Greek, Syriac and Latin read the following verb as an imperative while twelve manuscripts and four versions read a word meaning field where our text has breasts. Wesley says the women indulged in idleness, and dates the failure of the vintage to the Assyrian invasion.
Henry keeps the women and sharpens the charge, that to feed their pride and luxury their husbands and fathers were tempted to starve the poor.

positions.view: Provinces and cities, following the ancient paraphrase.
Possibly the men, for their effeminacy, or the cities of Judea; the readings are various.
The women of the pseudo-aristocracy, though the forms are masculine and the call is not limited to them.
Women literally, to feed whose luxury the poor were starved.

debates.question: Does the phrase about days and years mean long duration or quick arrival?

positions.view: Quick arrival, like the saying about a year and a day.
Long duration: the threat is of new afflictions after the first year, with no end held out.
Either the interval before the trouble or its continuance; the readings differ.

outliers.note: Explains the section's placement by the harem influence he takes to have stood behind the counsels of the king and his ministers.

themes: Rise up, ye women that are at ease; hear my voice, ye careless daughters; give ear unto my speech.
Many days and years shall ye be troubled, ye careless women: for the vintage shall fail, the gathering shall not come.
Tremble, ye women that are at ease; be troubled, ye careless ones: strip you, and make you bare, and gird sackcloth upon your loins.
They shall lament for the teats, for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine.
Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns and briers; yea, upon all the houses of joy in the joyous city:

14.pericope_label: Because the palaces shall be forsaken; the multitude of the city shall be left... And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever

schools.summary: Ellicott admires the bold pencil and rapid strokes of the outline and identifies the forts as those of Ophel, the fortified south-eastern slope of the temple mountain; he keeps to the structure of the prophecy, that there was a fixed limit to the desolation and that the prophet dwelt, as an earlier one had, on an outpouring which should sweep away the frivolities of a profligate luxury; and he sees outward blessings, themselves symbols of something beyond, giving place to spiritual ones, so that over the whole country the judgment and righteousness that had been lacking find a home. Delitzsch reads the prophet as congratulating his hearers in the face of a double judgment.

Gill notes that the word for palace is singular, so two rabbis take it for the king's palace while the ancient paraphrase makes it the temple, left desolate as Christ afterwards foretold; he argues from the length of the ruin that Pentecost cannot be the outpouring meant, since that fell before the destruction by the Romans while the Chaldean desolation had not lasted so long, so the pouring forth must be still to come, bringing in the fulness of the Gentiles and the conversion of the Jews; he widens the promise of judgment in the wilderness as far as it will go, to desert parts of the world where the Scriptures had no place; and he is satisfied with none of the possibilities for the work of righteousness, since the peace cannot arise from works done by men, there being no justification by these, nor quite from sanctification, though that comes nearer. Calvin is interested not in the building but the levelling, since nothing however splendid is exempt and men are dazzled by their own splendour and soothed to sleep amid their wealth; he explains that some hope had to be left them lest they faint; and he uses the promise of judgment against a misreading of Israel's hope, that the true condition of the Church is that justice and judgment prevail, so the Jews were not confined to transitory enjoyments as some fanatics imagine.

Clarke adds what made Ophel worth naming, that it rose higher than the rest of Zion at the eastern end, was strong by its situation, and had a wall of its own separating it from the city; he reports that fifteen manuscripts and two editions read the next word with the article, making it an appellative, a fruitful field rather than the mountain of that name; and on the last verse he reads the second noun as the culture of righteousness, so that righteousness cultivated by peace produces tranquillity of mind and permanent security, before turning from the text to address his reader directly. Wesley says the place is forsaken of God, the joy of wild asses being the desolate ground they delight in, and takes the opposite view of the outpouring from Gill's, that the word signifies to reveal and the promise was fully accomplished in the days of the Messiah.

debates.question: When is the Spirit poured out from on high?

positions.view: Still future, and not at Pentecost, since the ruin outlasted that; it will bring in the fulness of the Gentiles.
Fully accomplished in the days of the Messiah; the word properly means to reveal.
At a fixed limit set to the desolation, sweeping away a profligate luxury.
Whenever it comes, the promise is inserted so the people may not faint under the threat.

debates.question: What is the palace that shall be forsaken?

positions.view: The king's palace by one reading, the temple by the ancient paraphrase; the noun is singular.
Not the point: what matters is that nothing however splendid is exempt from the levelling.
Part of a rapid outline whose named forts are those of Ophel.

outliers.note: Breaks off from exposition to address the reader directly, asking whether he has the principle of righteousness and whether he cultivates it.

themes: Because the palaces shall be forsaken; the multitude of the city shall be left; the forts and towers shall be for dens for ever, a joy of wild asses, a pasture of flocks;
Until the spirit be poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness be a fruitful field, and the fruitful field be counted for a forest.
Then judgment shall dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness remain in the fruitful field.
And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever.

18.pericope_label: And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places... Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters, that send forth thither the feet of the ox and the ass

schools.summary: Ellicott would render the clause but it shall hail, taking the storm for a sharp judgment preceding the blessedness, and holds that the forest stands in prophetic symbolism for the rulers of a kingdom, elsewhere those of Assyria and here probably those of Judah; he knows the reading that keeps Assyria here and rejects it, since the city that follows is clearly Jerusalem, which shall be brought low, its pride humbled to the ground, in order that it may afterwards be exalted. On the closing benediction he gives the picture its final touch, the whole land irrigated by calmly flowing streams, men casting their seed broadcast, oxen and asses drawing the plough over rich ground, the country under tillage from end to end instead of the meagre pasturage of an earlier chapter or the thorns of this one, and adds that a spiritual meaning underlies the literal.

Gill keeps the peace outward, Jews and Gentiles dwelling together free from the outrages of the enemy when the spiritual reign of Christ comes; he makes the forest antichrist and the antichristian states, so called for their numbers and barrenness, and notes that a hailstorm sometimes falls by providence not on fields but on waste ground, as the plague fell on the Egyptians and not on Israel in Goshen; and he takes the closing benediction spiritually alone, addressing it to the ministers of the gospel in the latter day, the word compared to seed and the preachers to sowers who will sow among great multitudes. Calvin argues that since the righteousness in question has its seat in the hearts of men its fruit must have the same seat, so the peace is that of the apostle's saying that being justified by faith we have peace with God; he declines to name anyone for the forest, holding that the prophets describe the reign of Christ under metaphors borrowed from an earthly kingdom and that the meaning is simply that the Lord will make distresses fall elsewhere, and understanding by forest the desert places; and he measures the distance the promise covers, from a land overspread with thorns and levelled cities to a people called blessed.

Clarke keeps Assyria and guesses the city to be Nineveh or Babylon, though he calls the verse very obscure; on the last verse he ends in travel and natural history, reporting that a traveller's account of rice-growing answers it exactly, the seed being sown upon standing water and the flooded ground trodden by oxen and asses mid-leg deep before sowing, the young plants afterwards transplanted in the water, and adding from two other writers that rice is the food of two-thirds of mankind. Wesley reverses the earlier figure to get his answer, that as the blessing turns a wilderness into a fruitful field, so the judgment falls on those who were a fruitful field and are turned into a forest, the unbelieving Jews, the city being Jerusalem, which the prophet foresaw would be the great enemy of the Messiah.

debates.question: What does the hail fall on?

positions.view: The rulers and princes of Judah; the city that follows is clearly Jerusalem.
Assyria, the city being Nineveh or Babylon, though the verse is very obscure.
Antichrist and the antichristian states, barren as a forest is barren.
The unbelieving Jews, once a fruitful field and now turned into a forest.
Nobody in particular: desert places, the point being only that the distress is driven elsewhere.

debates.question: Is the closing benediction about farming or ministry?

positions.view: A golden age of agriculture, under which a spiritual meaning obviously lies.
Ministry alone: the word is the seed and gospel preachers are the sowers.
Real fertility, described by figures because plain language would not carry the change.
Literal rice cultivation, which the verse describes exactly.

outliers.note: Ends the chapter in agricultural travel writing, matching the verse to the flooding and treading of rice fields and noting that rice feeds two-thirds of mankind.

themes: And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places;
When it shall hail, coming down on the forest; and the city shall be low in a low place.
Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters, that send forth thither the feet of the ox and the ass.
